name: Zurich Reformation
description: The Zurich Reformation rejected Roman Catholic authority and practices under Zwingli, leading to a break from the Catholic Church.
narrative: The Zurich Reformation rejected Roman Catholic authority and practices under Zwingli, leading to a break from the Catholic Church. Zwingli’s biblical preaching and disputes about church practice drew the city council into reform. Public disputations in 1523 authorized Scripture-centered preaching and helped dismantle older religious arrangements. Civil government and church life remained closely entangled; reform also provoked conflict with Anabaptists and Catholic cantons. The node represents a local historical stream, not the entire present Protestant Church in Switzerland.

key_figures.role: Zurich preacher and reformer
key_figures.summary: A Zurich preacher who advanced Scripture-based reform with civic support and developed a distinctive account of the Lord’s Supper.

key_figures.role: later Zurich reformer associated with the wider Swiss confessional tradition
key_figures.summary: Zwingli’s successor in the Zurich Reformed tradition, associated with the later Second Helvetic Confession and wider Reformed connections.

name: Genevan Reformation
description: The Genevan Reformation replaced Roman Catholicism with Reformed Christianity in Geneva.
narrative: The Genevan Reformation replaced Roman Catholicism with Reformed Christianity in Geneva. Geneva’s civic and religious changes opened a setting for Reformed teaching, but the relationship between pastors and magistrates remained contested. Calvin’s return in 1541 led to ordinances organizing ministry and discipline. Refugees, pastoral training, publishing, and contact with other countries spread Geneva’s influence. This was a city-based church order and a teaching center, not a global denomination controlled by one reformer.

key_figures.summary: A French Reformed theologian and Genevan pastor whose writing and church ordinances influenced communities well beyond Geneva.

key_figures.role: evangelist and reforming organizer in Geneva
key_figures.summary: evangelist and reforming organizer in Geneva. This role should be read in the formation and development described above, rather than as a claim of sole authorship of the tradition.

name: Scottish Reformation
description: The Scottish Reformation broke Scotland away from the Roman Catholic Church and established a Protestant national church.
narrative: The Scottish Reformation broke Scotland away from the Roman Catholic Church and established a Protestant national church. Criticism of medieval religious practice joined the preaching of reformers and the political struggle over Scotland’s future. Knox and colleagues produced a confession approved by Parliament in 1560; parliamentary acts rejected papal authority and the Mass. Reformers understood this as reforming the church rather than inventing Christianity in Scotland. A full Presbyterian court system developed later, so it should not be assumed complete at the first constitutional break.

key_figures.summary: A Scottish reformer whose ministry in England and Geneva influenced his preaching, worship, and church reform in Scotland.

name: Church of Scotland established
description: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament repudiated papal authority, establishing the Church of Scotland as a national Protestant church separate from Rome.
narrative: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament repudiated papal authority, establishing the Church of Scotland as a national Protestant church separate from Rome. The Reformation of 1560 supplied a Protestant confession and transformed existing church structures. Presbyterian government developed through later struggles over royal authority and episcopacy, with a full system recognized in 1592. Westminster became a principal doctrinal standard in 1647. From January 2026 a Book of Confessions adds other historic and contemporary statements, making a Westminster-only description of current standards incomplete.

name: English Reformation
description: The English Reformation broke from Roman Catholic authority and established a national church under royal supremacy.
narrative: The English Reformation broke from Roman Catholic authority and established a national church under royal supremacy. Henry VIII’s dispute over his marriage coincided with a struggle over jurisdiction and royal power. Parliamentary acts in the 1530s transferred authority from Rome to the crown. Further Protestant reform, Catholic restoration, and Elizabethan settlement followed under successive monarchs. The process cannot be reduced to one fully Protestant church springing into existence in 1534: political separation and doctrinal reform proceeded at different speeds.

name: Marian exile congregation
description: English and Scottish Protestant exiles formed the English Congregation in Geneva during the Marian exile period.
narrative: English and Scottish Protestant exiles formed the English Congregation in Geneva during the Marian exile period. Religious repression under Mary I drove English and Scottish Protestants into continental exile. A congregation gathered in Geneva in the mid-1550s, where John Knox and other ministers adapted Reformed worship to their community. Its practices and scriptural discussion helped transmit Genevan patterns back to Britain. When political conditions changed, the exile congregation dispersed; its significance continued through people and texts rather than a permanent denomination.

name: Lutheran Reformation
description: The Lutheran Reformation emerged in opposition to Roman Catholic doctrine and authority, beginning in 1517.
narrative: The Lutheran Reformation emerged in opposition to Roman Catholic doctrine and authority, beginning in 1517. Luther’s controversy over indulgences expanded into disputes about salvation, authority, and church practice. Reform was transmitted through preaching, vernacular teaching, print, and political protection. The 1517 date is a conventional opening milestone; regional churches took institutional form over subsequent decades. The movement did not produce one worldwide denomination, and later Lutheran churches developed different political and confessional arrangements.

name: Geneva exile congregation model
description: The English Congregation in Geneva (led mainly by John Knox) modeled Presbyterian worship and governance, providing a Genevan pattern that influenced later Scottish polity.
narrative: The English Congregation in Geneva (led mainly by John Knox) modeled Presbyterian worship and governance, providing a Genevan pattern that influenced later Scottish polity. The Scottish Reformation created demand for a church order accountable through elders and assemblies rather than royal or episcopal control alone. Structures emerged unevenly, and disputes with monarchs continued for generations. The dataset uses 1581 for early presbyteries; official church history places recognition of the full system in 1592. This node is a governance tradition, not a separate denomination founded to teach another gospel.

name: Scottish/Ulster migration
description: Colonial Presbyterianism originated in part through immigrants from the Church of Scotland and Presbyterians from Ireland to the American colonies.
narrative: Colonial Presbyterianism originated in part through immigrants from the Church of Scotland and Presbyterians from Ireland to the American colonies. Migrants and ministers from Scotland, Ulster, and other backgrounds brought Reformed worship and church order to colonial settlements. They needed congregations, trained ministry, and mutual accountability in a setting without one national Presbyterian establishment. Francis Makemie’s arrival in 1683 and the 1706 presbytery are useful markers. Migration itself was not an ecclesiastical corporation, and a count of migrants should not be confused with denominational membership.

name: First American presbytery
description: In 1706 seven ministers organized the Presbytery of Philadelphia and chose Francis Makemie as moderator, formalizing Presbyterian polity in the colonies.
narrative: In 1706 seven ministers organized the Presbytery of Philadelphia and chose Francis Makemie as moderator, formalizing Presbyterian polity in the colonies. Scattered colonial ministers needed mutual support, discipline, and a way to coordinate preaching and church life. The formation of a presbytery provided that connection without creating a state church. Makemie was a leading participant, but several ministers shared the work. The year is well established while the exact first meeting date is less secure because early records are incomplete. Later synods and national assemblies built on this organizational setting.

name: National PCUSA formed
description: The Presbyterian Church in the United States of America was organized in 1789 as the first national Presbyterian denomination, building on colonial presbyteries and synods.
narrative: The Presbyterian Church in the United States of America was organized in 1789 as the first national Presbyterian denomination, building on colonial presbyteries and synods. Colonial presbyteries and synods developed national structures after American independence. Constitutional organization in 1788 and the first General Assembly in 1789 are distinct milestones. Subsequent disputes over revival, theology, slavery, and mission produced separations and reunions. Calling the entire 1789 body simply northern projects a later sectional identity backward. It joined the UPCNA in 1958 rather than becoming the present PCUSA directly.
